text: Goodwill Zwelithini kaBhekuzulu (27 July 1948 – 12 March 2021) served as the King of the Zulu Nation from 1968 until his death in 2021. He became king at the age of 20 following the death of his father, King Cyprian Bhekuzulu, in 1968, with Prince Israel Mcwayizeni acting as regent from 1968 to 1971 while Zwelithini took refuge in the then Transkei province of South Africa to avoid assassination. After turning 21 and marrying, Zwelithini was formally installed as the eighth monarch of the Zulus at a traditional ceremony in Nongoma on 3 December 1971, attended by 20,000 people. He died on 12 March 2021, aged 72, after being admitted to hospital for a diabetes-related illness; during funeral preparations, his traditional prime minister, Mangosuthu Buthelezi, announced he had died of COVID-19. During the 1990s power vacuum following the end of Apartheid and White South African dominance, the king became increasingly involved in partisan politics. The Zulu-dominated Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) opposed parts of the new constitution proposed by the African National Congress (ANC) regarding Zulu internal governance, particularly advocating for an autonomous and sovereign Zulu king as constitutional head of state. As a result, the IFP did not register for the 1994 election until the king’s role in the new democracy was clarified. Mandela and President De Klerk arranged a special meeting, agreeing that international mediators would resolve the dispute, leading to the IFP’s registration and its demonstration of political strength by securing the majority of provincial votes in KwaZulu-Natal during that election. Although the constitution makes the king’s role largely ceremonial, he is required to act on the official advice of the provincial premier. On occasion, President Nelson Mandela sought to bypass the IFP by making direct overtures to the king, such as when Mandela’s daughter, Zeni, married Prince Thumbumuzi Dlamini, a brother of King Zwelithini’s Great Wife, Queen Mantfombi. Despite this, the IFP remained in power in the province until 2003. Throughout most of his reign, his cousin (uncle in Zulu reckoning), Mangosuthu Buthelezi, Prince of KwaPhindangene and founder of the IFP, served as Zulu prime minister. However, in September 1994, tensions between the two escalated as the annual Shaka Zulu celebration approached, with rumors that the king intended to replace Buthelezi with former regent Prince Mcwayizeni, who had joined the ANC in 1990, after announcing Buthelezi would no longer be his chief advisor and canceling the holiday ceremony. For his safety, federal troops escorted the king by helicopter to Johannesburg. Although Buthelezi was serving as Minister of Home Affairs, Mandela’s reconciliation efforts failed. Buthelezi moved the event to Stanger and addressed 10,000 Zulu supporters. Later, when Prince Sifiso Zulu was being interviewed on television by the South African Broadcasting Corporation, Buthelezi and his bodyguards forcibly interrupted the program, physically intimidating the prince, drawing national attention and prompting a public rebuke from Mandela, after which Buthelezi apologized to the Zulu Royal Family, Cabinet, and nation. Relations between Zwelithini and Buthelezi later improved. The king cooperated with the ANC since it took over government in KwaZulu-Natal, and his finances are controlled by KwaZulu-Natal provincial authorities. In 1989, he criticized ANC leadership for not inviting him and Buthelezi to a rally welcoming back Rivonia Trial defendants released after nearly three decades. As constitutional monarch of KwaZulu-Natal, he was head of the Ubukhosi, the state-recognized institution of Traditional Leadership, and chaired the Usuthu Tribal Authority and Nongoma Regional Authority established under the KwaZulu Amakhosi and Iziphakanyiswa Act. In his address at the opening of the Provincial Parliament on 28 September 2003, he urged the government and legislators to recognize the Ubukhosi, noting that traditional leaders are not consulted in policy-making affecting their daily lives, and that the institution has existed since time immemorial and survived colonial regimes. He emphasized that traditional leadership symbolizes community solidarity and that abandoning it in a democratic government would be a pipe-dream, citing neighboring countries that had dismantled such institutions post-independence and later regretted it. He also praised Buthelezi for championing traditional leadership in South Africa. As chairman of the Ingonyama Trust, a corporate entity managing land traditionally owned by the king, he oversaw 32% of KwaZulu-Natal’s area. As custodian of Zulu traditions, he revived cultural events such as the Umhlanga, a reed dance promoting moral awareness and AIDS education among Zulu women, and the Ukweshwama, a traditional ceremony involving the killing of a bull, which in November 2009 led to a lawsuit by Animal Rights Africa alleging cruelty. He traveled extensively abroad to promote tourism and trade in KwaZulu-Natal and to fundraise for Zulu-supported charities, often accompanied by one of his queens consort, and was officially hosted by local Zulu organizations and granted audiences to Zulus living abroad. In June 1994, the University of Zululand conferred upon him an honorary doctorate in agriculture; he served as Chancellor of the South African branch of Newport University and received an honorary doctorate in law from Coker College of South Carolina in March 1999. In the first half of 2001, he was inaugurated as Chancellor of the ML Sultan Technikon in KwaZulu-Natal. His authorized biography, *King of Goodwill*, was published in 2003, and its musical dramatization premiered at the Market Theatre, Johannesburg on 16 March 2005. In 2004, he spoke at The Synagogue Church Of All Nations in Lagos, Nigeria, on trade and peace. In January 2012, during a commemoration of the 133rd anniversary of the Battle of Isandlwana, he made controversial remarks stating that same-sex relations were "rotten," which were condemned by the South African Human Rights Commission and LGBT rights groups, and rebuked by President Jacob Zuma. The Zulu Royal Household later clarified that the comments were mistranslated and that the king had expressed concern about moral decay in South Africa, including widespread male-on-male sexual abuse, not condemned same-sex relations. In September 2012, King Zwelithini requested R18 million from the KwaZulu-Natal government to build new property, including a R6 million palace for his youngest wife, Queen Mafu, and upgrades to Queen MaMchiza’s palace. The royal household’s CFO, Mduduzi Mthembu, stated the funds were needed. The department also requested $1.4 million USD for improvements to Queen MaMchiza’s palace. The government had already budgeted around $6.9 million USD for the royal family in 2012, prompting accusations of lavish spending; in 2008, opposition parties criticized the king’s wives for spending approximately $24,000 USD on linen, designer clothes, and expensive holidays. At a community meeting in Phongolo UPhongolo Local Municipality in March 2015, the king acknowledged that while other nations contributed to South Africa’s liberation, this should not justify foreigners causing economic inconvenience by competing with locals for scarce opportunities. He claimed he was free to speak where politicians were not, urging foreigners to return to their native lands, asserting that South Africans in diaspora had not opened businesses abroad. These remarks were made during a period of rising tensions between South Africans and non-nationals, following violence in Soweto in January that spread to KwaZulu-Natal, resulting in three deaths. The Democratic Alliance’s spokesman called for a public retraction and apology, criticizing the remarks as "highly irresponsible," while a SAHRC official labeled them xenophobic in light of recent attacks on foreigners. Allegedly sparking violence against non-nationals, the king’s comments did not distinguish between legal and illegal immigrants, and his spokesman later clarified he was referring only to those present in the country illegally. King Goodwill Zwelithini had six wives and around 40 children.
